title: The Night We Almost Broke
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 33 of 40
content:
The worst fight we ever had began because Aang volunteered our house.

He did not mean to.

That mattered later.

It did not matter first.

A delegation from the eastern district had lost its meeting hall in the storm. Aang, trying to be helpful, told them they could use our courtyard for weekly assemblies until repairs were finished.

He told us at dinner.

Toph stopped chewing.

Katara set down her spoon.

I stared at him.

Aang’s smile disappeared.

“What?”

Toph’s chair scraped back.

“No.”

“I thought—”

“That’s the problem.”

Aang looked toward Katara.

She did not rescue him.

“Our home is not public space,” she said.

“I know.”

“Apparently not.”

His face tightened.

“I was trying to help. Their hall is gone.”

“So find them a hall,” Toph snapped.

“There isn’t one available.”

“That doesn’t make ours theirs.”

Aang looked at me.

I hated that I saw the question there.

Not because he expected me to agree.

Because he was suddenly counting votes in our kitchen.

I stood.

“No.”

His face fell.

“Okay.”

The quick surrender should have ended it.

Instead it made me angrier.

“You don’t get to say okay like the problem is solved.”

Aang blinked.

“I agreed.”

“After you already told them yes.”

“I’ll tell them no.”

“And we get to be the reason.”

“I won’t say that.”

“You don’t have to.”

Katara’s voice was low.

“They’ll know.”

Aang stood too.

“What do you want me to do? I made a mistake.”

Toph laughed sharply.

“A mistake is forgetting milk.”

“I said I’m sorry.”

“You didn’t.”

Silence.

Aang’s mouth opened.

Closed.

Toph was right.

He had explained.

He had agreed to reverse it.

He had not apologized.

Aang’s frustration showed now.

“I’m sorry.”

The words came too hard.

Toph heard that.

Of course she did.

“Great apology.”

Katara said, “Toph.”

“No. Everybody keeps acting like because he’s trying, we have to make it easy for him when his public life swallows our private one.”

Aang’s face changed.

“That’s not fair.”

Toph stood.

“The courtyard was one of my conditions for moving in.”

“I know.”

“Ground access. Private house. No official Avatar residence.”

“I know.”

“Then why didn’t you remember?”

Aang had no answer.

That was worse than any answer.

Toph walked out.

Katara followed her.

I stayed.

That was my mistake.

Not because Aang did not deserve somebody to stay.

Because I stayed for the wrong reason.

The room was unbearable. Aang looked wrecked. My instinct rose immediately: make it manageable. Translate. Soften. Solve.

I began collecting bowls.

Aang said, “Don’t.”

I froze.

He looked at me.

“Please don’t clean because you don’t know what to say.”

I set down the bowl.

That hurt because it was accurate.

“I’m angry too.”

“I know.”

“No.” My voice sharpened. “You know Toph is angry. Katara is angry. I’m the one still standing here, so you’re treating me like the safer one.”

Aang stared.

The words kept coming.

“I asked for a room with a door because I needed part of this house not to belong to your work. Toph asked for the courtyard. Katara asked for a home where public need didn’t decide everything. We wrote it down.”

“I forgot.”

“Yes.”

He flinched.

I hated that I wanted to take the words back.

I did not.

Aang sank into his chair.

“I don’t know how to do this.”

“Neither do we.”

“No, I mean…” He pressed both palms to his eyes. “Everywhere I go, people need something. If I can help and I don’t, I feel like I’m failing.”

Compassion.

Duty.

The traits I loved in him turning sharp inside our home.

“And if helping them means volunteering us?”

“I didn’t think.”

“I know.”

“That sounds worse every time.”

“It does.”

He laughed once, miserable.

I sat across from him.

For several minutes, neither of us spoke.

Then Aang said, “I keep thinking the Avatar’s job is to say yes to suffering.”

I looked at him.

“What does that mean?”

“If I see a need, I’m supposed to move toward it.”

“That sounds noble.”

“It’s killing my ability to notice what it costs other people.”

There it was.

Not absolution.

Recognition.

Before I could answer, the front door opened.

Katara came in alone.

“Where’s Toph?” Aang asked.

“Academy.”

His face tightened.

“She said she’s sleeping there.”

The room changed.

Aang stood.

Katara held up one hand.

“Do not go after her.”

“I need to apologize.”

“She told me she needs space.”

Aang stopped.

I watched duty collide with consent in his face.

He sat back down.

Good.

Katara remained standing.

“I’m angry at you,” she said.

“I know.”

She pointed at him. “And stop saying that like knowledge is repair.”

I almost laughed because she had said nearly the same thing to me months earlier.

Aang nodded.

“You’re right.”

Katara’s eyes filled.

“I have spent years watching the world take pieces of you because you let it.”

He looked down.

“And I love that you care. I do. But sometimes I hate the Avatar.”

Aang looked up sharply.

Katara’s tears spilled.

“Not you. The role. The thing that walks into our meals and our bed and every plan we make.”

Aang’s face crumpled.

I stood instinctively.

Then stopped.

Nobody needed me to interrupt this with comfort.

Katara wiped her cheeks.

“I hate that saying this feels selfish.”

“It isn’t,” Aang whispered.

“I know.”

This time the phrase meant something different.

She sat.

The three of us stayed at the table until the food went cold.

Nobody slept much.

At dawn, Toph still had not returned.

Aang went to the courtyard and stood at the threshold as if the stones themselves had become an accusation.

I found him there.

“I could lose all of you.”

The fear was naked.

“Yes.”

He looked at me.

It was not the answer he wanted.

It was the answer our household agreement required.

Any of us could leave.

Choice only meant something if departure remained possible.

Aang closed his eyes.

“I hate that.”

“So do I.”

“What do I do?”

“You wait until Toph wants to talk.”

“And then?”

“You apologize without asking her to make you feel better.”

He nodded.

“And after that?”

“We figure out whether this was a break or a crack.”

Aang looked toward the street.

For once, he could not bend the problem.

Katara could not heal it.

Toph could not force it into another shape.

I could not file it into order.

By evening, our four-bowl table had three people sitting around it.

The fourth bowl stayed in the cupboard.

Nobody set it out as a symbol.

That would have been pressure too.

We ate quietly.

The house felt wrong.

Not empty.

Uncertain.

Love had survived riots, storms, public scrutiny, grief, injury, and politics.

None of those guaranteed it would survive us.

That was the night I finally understood that commitment was not the certainty that nobody would leave.

It was the willingness to change what made leaving necessary—without demanding that change purchase forgiveness.

For the next two days, we communicated like diplomats from hostile nations.

Katara left notes about meals.

Aang answered practical questions with painful politeness.

Toph spent more time at the academy than necessary.

I worked late and told myself it was because the charter rewrite mattered.

The house became efficient and unbearable.

On the third evening I found Aang sitting alone on the roof.

I almost went back downstairs.

He heard me anyway.

“You don’t have to stay.”

The sentence hurt because it was exactly what we were fighting about.

I sat several feet away.

“I know.”

Wind moved between us.

Aang’s voice was quiet. “I keep thinking if I can make enough room for people, then nobody has to be turned away.”

“Our house is not a nation.”

“I know.”

“You keep saying that after you act like it is.”

He flinched.

I wanted to take the words back because I loved him.

I left them there because I loved him.

After a while he said, “When the monks raised me, private space worked differently. People came and went. We slept in shared rooms. Guests were…” He stopped. “That doesn’t mean I get to make that your rule.”

“No.”

“I thought generosity was always good.”

“It can still be generous. Just not with something that belongs to all of us.”

He nodded.

Downstairs, a door opened. Toph’s footsteps crossed the hall, then stopped directly beneath us.

“She’s listening,” I said.

“I know.”

“Stop having productive conflict without us!” Toph shouted through the roof.

Aang laughed unexpectedly.

So did I.

The fight was not over.

But for the first time since it began, the house sounded like ours again.

Before we went downstairs, Aang asked, “Do you want me to apologize now or after everyone’s here?”

“After.”

“Okay.”

He did. Not beautifully. Not defensively either.

That mattered more.

Downstairs, the four of us finished the conversation. It took hours. Nobody won. The house felt more secure for it.

Nobody mistook that for failure again.
